p01.title: Simple hello
p01.statement:
Read a name from the input (one line of text) and print it exactly in this form:

`Hello, NAME`

`NAME` is replaced by the name from the input. There must be exactly **one space** between the comma and the name.

Do not put a message inside `input(...)`; write only `input()`.
hints: The output is one line made of two parts: the fixed text `Hello,` and the name the user typed.
The comma after `Hello` must be inside the text. When `print` gets two arguments, it puts one space between them by itself.
mistakes: Writing a message inside `input`, like `input("Name?")`: that text is printed too and adds extra output.
Converting the name to a number with `int(name)`: for a name, `int` gives an error, and the output must be the same text.

solutions.name: Method 1: print with two arguments
steps: We read one line of text (the name) from the input with `input()`.
We store the name in a variable called `name`.
With `print` we give two parts: the text `"Hello,"` and the name itself.
explain: This method uses a feature of `print`: if we give it several things separated by commas, it prints them side by side with one space. The comma after `Hello` is inside the quotes, so it is part of the text.
The important point is not to write the space after the comma yourself. If you write `"Hello, "` with a space and `print` adds a space as well, the output has two spaces and the test fails.

solutions.name: Method 2: building one text with +
steps: We read the name from the input and put it in `name`.
With `+` we join the text `"Hello, "` (with one space at the end) to the name.
We put the result in the variable `message` and print it with one `print`.
explain: In this method we build the whole text ourselves. The `+` sign joins two strings and adds nothing to them. That is why the space must be inside the first string.
Since we already have one complete text, a single `print` is enough, and `print` itself adds no space.

p02.title: Three lines in a row
p02.statement:
Read three lines of text from the input and print the same three lines **in exactly the same order** (each input line → one output line).

Do not add or remove anything; do not put a message inside `input`.
hints: You do not need to store all the lines; read each line and print it right away with `print`.
Call `input` without a message; whatever text you write inside it appears in the output and the test fails.
p02.guideTitle: Three lines in a row — input and print

solutions.name: Method 1: three inputs and three prints
steps: We write `input()` three times and put each line in its own variable.
We write `print` three times and print each variable in order.
explain: Each `input()` reads one line of the input and returns it as text. Since we have three lines, we write `input()` three times and keep each one in a separate variable.
Each `print` gives one line of output. So three `print`s produce three separate lines. The `print`s must be in the same order as the input.

solutions.name: Method 2: a for loop that repeats three times
steps: `range(3)` means the loop runs three times.
On each run of the loop we read one line of input.
We print that same line immediately.
explain: When we do not use the loop counter inside the loop body, we can name it `_`. `range(3)` gives three repeats, and on each repeat one line is read and printed.
This method is much easier for more lines, because we only change the number inside `range`.

p31.title: Name and age
p31.statement:
Read two input lines: the first is the **name** (one English word) and the second is the **age** (an integer).

The output must be exactly this form:

`Ali is 20 years old`

That is: the name, then the word `is`, then the age, and at the end `years old`; **one space** between all the parts.
hints: The first input is the name and the second is the age; read both with `input()` and print the age as it is.
The output must be exactly `Ali is 20 years old`; `print` with several arguments puts a space between them, so do not write an extra space.
p31.guideTitle: Name and age — print with several parts, and str
mistakes: `Ali is` without enough space: if we stick `"is"` on without a space on both sides, the output becomes `Aliis`.

solutions.name: Method 1: print with commas
steps: We read the name with `input()`.
We read the age with `input()` too (the same text is enough).
With `print` we give the four parts separated by commas; `print` itself puts the spaces.
explain: `input()` always returns text. To print the age we do not need to turn it into a number; we print the same text.
Each `print` argument separated by a comma is printed with one space. The texts `"is"` and `"years old"` are inside quotes so that they are part of the output.

solutions.name: Method 2: building a text with + and str
steps: We read the name.
We turn the age into a number with `int` and then back into text with `str` so that it can be joined with `+`.
We build the whole text with `+` and print it once.
explain: Because `+` only joins text to text, we turned the numeric age into text with `str`. If we did not, Python would give an error.
Here the spaces are inside the strings (`" is "`). So we must write them exactly; one space too few or too many fails the test.

p03.title: Sum of two numbers
p03.statement:
Read two integers:

- first line: the first number
- second line: the second number

Print their sum on one line.
hints: `input()` always returns a string; convert the numbers with `int` before adding them.
If you put two strings next to each other with `+`, the result is stuck together; the numbers must be added.
p03.guideTitle: Sum of two numbers — reading numbers and the + operator

solutions.name: Method 1: read two numbers and add with +
steps: We read the first number with `input()` and turn it into a number with `int(...)`.
We repeat the same for the second number.
With `print(a + b)` we print the sum on one line.
explain: `input()` always returns text, even if the user typed a number. If we put the text `3` and the text `5` together with +, we get `35`, not 8. That is why we turn each input into a number with `int` and then add.

The reading order matters: the first input line goes into the variable `a` and the second into `b`. Addition of two numbers is commutative, so the order of adding does not change the result, but we must read the inputs in the order the user enters them.

solutions.name: Method 2: read two numbers into a list
steps: We make an empty list to hold the numbers.
With a for loop we read a number twice and add each one to the list.
We add the first and the second element of the list and print the result.
explain: A list is an ordered collection of values. With `append` a new value is added at its end. When we keep the numbers in a list, we can reach them with the indexes 0 and 1.

The loop `for _ in range(2)` repeats exactly twice. The variable `_` means the repeat number does not matter to us. This method is overkill for a problem as simple as this one, but the same pattern is useful in problems with more numbers.

p04.title: Remainder of a division
p04.statement:
Read two **positive** integers:

- first line: `a`
- second line: `b`

Print the remainder of dividing `a` by `b` (the same as `a % b`).
hints: `a % b` is the remainder of `a` divided by `b`; do not swap `a` and `b`.
Read the two numbers on two separate lines and convert each one with `int` right away.
p04.guideTitle: Remainder of a division — the % operator

solutions.name: Method 1: the % operator (remainder)
steps: We read the two positive numbers `a` and `b` from the input.
With the `%` operator we calculate the remainder of dividing `a` by `b`.
We print the result with `print`.
explain: The `%` operator returns the remainder, that is, what is left after dividing `a` by `b` completely. For example 17 % 5 is 2, because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.

Since `a` and `b` are positive, the behaviour of `%` in this problem is exactly what we need. If the numbers were negative, Python gives the remainder the sign of the divisor; this problem does not ask for that case.

solutions.name: Method 2: with the integer quotient and subtraction
steps: With the `//` operator we calculate the integer quotient of `a` divided by `b`.
We multiply the quotient by `b` and subtract it from `a`.
The result is the remainder.
explain: Every number can be written as "dividend = quotient × divisor + remainder". If we take the quotient with `//`, the remainder is `a - q × b`. This method shows what the `%` operator does.
This method is good for learning the idea, but in practice `%` is simpler and more readable. If `b` is zero, both methods give an error, and this problem does not ask for `b` being zero.

p47.title: Counting the words of a sentence
p47.statement:
Read one line, an English sentence. The words are separated by **one space**.

Print the number of words in the sentence.
hints: Break the text into words with `split()`; the number of words is the `len` of the list.
`split()` without an argument works with any number of spaces; so do not worry about extra spaces.
p47.guideTitle: Counting the words of a sentence — split and a loop
mistakes: Counting characters instead of words: `len(text)` gives the number of letters and spaces, not words.

solutions.name: Method 1: separating the words with split
steps: We read the whole sentence line with `input()`.
With `split()` we turn the sentence into a list of words; `split` without an argument separates at spaces.
With `len` we count the words and print the count.
explain: `split()` without an argument breaks the text at spaces and builds a list of words. For example `hello world` becomes `['hello', 'world']`. `len` gives the number of members of this list.

Since the problem says the words are separated by one space, this method is exact. If there were several spaces in a row, `split()` without an argument would count them as one; that feature works in our favour.

solutions.name: Method 2: counting the starts of words with a loop
steps: We start a counter at zero.
We read the sentence letter by letter. Wherever a letter is not a space and the previous letter was a space, a word has started.
In that case we add one to the counter.
explain: This method is written without `split` to show how a word is recognised in a text: a word starts where a non-space letter comes after a space. The variable `previous` keeps the previous letter.

In the loop `for ch in line` every character of the sentence is seen once. The important point is to update `previous` at the end of each round; otherwise we keep comparing with the very first letter.

p87.title: String length function
p87.statement:
Write a function named `word_length(text)` that returns the **number of letters** of the string `text` (spaces are counted too).

This problem is a **function test**.
hints: The function `len` gives the length of a string.
If you want to calculate it without `len`, loop over the string with `for` and count.
p87.guideTitle: String length function — return and len
mistakes: Ignoring the spaces when counting: the length of `a b` is three, not two.

solutions.name: Method 1: a function with len
steps: We define a function named `word_length` with one parameter `text`.
With `len(text)` we get the number of characters in the string.
With `return` we give that number back.
explain: A function is defined with `def` and gives a value back to whoever called it with `return`. In this problem the function prints nothing; it only returns the number so that the test can check it.
For a string, `len` gives the number of characters. The empty string has length zero, and spaces count as one character each. These two points are checked in the tests.

solutions.name: Method 2: a function that counts in a loop
steps: In the function we start a counter at zero.
For each character of the string we add one to the counter.
At the end we return the counter.
explain: This method does what `len` does inside: it sees each character once and counts it. Seeing it helps us understand that `len` is not magic; it is just a count.
The loop `for ch in text` does not run even once for an empty string, so `count` stays zero and the function returns zero; that is exactly the correct result the test expects.

p95.title: Length and uppercase of a word
p95.statement:
Read one English word (without spaces).

On the **first line** print the number of letters of the word, and on the **second line** print the same word in capital letters.
hints: The function `len` gives the number of letters of a string.
`upper()` turns a string into capital letters.
p95.guideTitle: Length and uppercase of a word — len and upper
mistakes: Swapping the order of the lines: first the length, then the capital letters.

solutions.name: Method 1: len and upper
steps: We read the word with `input()`.
With `len` we print the length of the word; this is the first print.
With `upper()` we make the same word in capital letters and print it; this is the second print.
explain: Each `print` prints a new line. So with two `print`s we have two output lines: first the length, then the capitalised word. The order of printing must be exactly this.
`upper()` works on a string and returns a new string; `word` itself does not change. That is why we print the result directly.

solutions.name: Method 2: counting letters with a loop and capitalising by hand
steps: We read the word and set a counter for the letters.
With a loop we count each letter.
To build the capital version, we capitalise the lowercase English letters one by one with `upper()` and put them side by side.
explain: In this method each letter is capitalised separately and added to the string `big`. This shows that `upper` works on a single letter too, and the final string is the sum of the capital letters.
If the input string is empty, `big` stays empty and the loop does not run. This method is slower than `upper()`, but it is good for learning loops and building strings.

p96.title: Counting the letter a in a word
p96.statement:
Read one English word (without spaces).

Print the number of **a** letters (lowercase) inside the word.
hints: Loop over the word with `for` and compare each letter with `"a"`.
If the word has no `a`, the answer is `0`.
p96.guideTitle: Counting the letter a in a word — a loop and an index
mistakes: Comparing with `=` instead of `==`: you cannot compare it with `=`; that is an assignment.

solutions.name: Method 1: a while loop with an index
steps: We read the word with `input()` and set a counter to zero.
We start an index `i` at zero and continue as long as `i` is smaller than the length of the word.
If the letter at place `i` is `a`, we add one to the counter; then we move `i` forward by one.
explain: In Python every string is like a list of letters that starts at place zero. `word[i]` gives the letter at place `i`. With a `while` loop we visit all the places one by one until we reach `len(word)`.
The important point is to move `i` forward by one at the end of each round; if we forget, the loop never ends. We distinguish lowercase `a` from capital `A`, as the problem asks.

solutions.name: Method 2: a for loop and if
steps: We set a counter to zero.
We read the word letter by letter.
If the letter equals `a`, we add one to the counter.
explain: This method shows the same logic with `for`: each letter is compared with `a` and, if equal, the counter grows. The `==` comparison is done between two one-letter strings.
Since the comparison is case-sensitive, `A` is not equal to `a` and is not counted, which is exactly what is asked.

p06.title: Even or odd
p06.statement:
Read an integer.

- if it is even, print exactly `even`
- if it is odd, print exactly `odd`

The output is only that one English word in lowercase (no extra space).
Note: the number `0` is even.
hints: Being even means the remainder of dividing by `2` is zero; the number `0` is even too.
The output is only `even` or `odd` in lowercase; do not print any extra text or space.
mistakes: Writing `=` instead of `==` in the condition: `=` means assignment, and `==` means comparison.

solutions.name: Method 1: if and else
steps: We read the number and convert it to an integer.
We calculate the remainder of dividing by 2 with `%`.
If the remainder is zero we print `even`, otherwise we print `odd`.
explain: Being even means being divisible by 2, that is, the remainder of dividing by 2 is zero. The number `0` is even too, because `0 % 2` is zero.
`if` checks the condition and, if it is true, the block inside it runs. `else` is for the false case.

solutions.name: Method 2: we check the odd case first
steps: We read the number.
If the remainder of dividing by 2 is 1, the number is odd and we print `odd`.
Otherwise the number is even and we print `even`.
explain: We tried the same logic from the other side. Both methods are correct; what matters is writing the condition correctly.
This method works for negative numbers too, because `-3 % 2` is `1`.
